stem: In plain terms, what does attention let each token do?
options: Skip ahead to see the answer
Look at the earlier tokens, weight which ones matter, and blend in what it took
Store the token for the next API call
Look up the token's definition in a dictionary
explanation: 'Look back, weight, blend' — computed fresh in every layer for every input. This is the mechanism behind 'context'.

stem: 'bank' near 'interest rate' and 'bank' near 'river' are the same token id. How can the model treat them differently?
options: The tokeniser assigns different ids based on the sentence
The model keeps two copies of every ambiguous word
It cannot — this is a known failure
Attention rewrites each token's vector using its neighbours, so the same id gets different vectors in different contexts
explanation: In a transformer every token's representation is computed in context. That is why one embedding table can serve many meanings.

stem: Attention compares every token with every earlier token. What follows for cost?
options: Cost falls as prompts get longer
Cost is constant regardless of length
Attention work grows roughly with the square of the prompt length — long prompts are disproportionately expensive
Only output tokens cost anything
explanation: The rest of the network is linear, so the whole is between linear and quadratic — but long context is never free.

stem: Where does the 'memory' in a multi-turn chat actually live?
options: In the KV cache on the provider's servers, permanently
In the prompt — your application re-sends the history every call
Inside the model between calls
In the tokeniser
explanation: There is no state between calls. Nothing persists unless your code sends it again.

stem: A key fact sits in the middle of a 60k-token prompt and the answer ignores it. Which explanation fits this lesson?
options: Attention is diluted across many tokens and biased toward the start and end of the prompt
The tokeniser dropped the middle
The model's weights were updated mid-request
Middle tokens are cheaper and therefore skipped
explanation: Position is an input; very long prompts show weaker attention to the middle. Retrieve just the passage, or move it to the edges (Lesson 2.5).

stem: Why are 'time to first token' and 'tokens per second' separate metrics?
options: The prompt is processed in parallel (fast), then output tokens are produced one loop iteration at a time (slow)
Providers report whichever is smaller
Only one applies to streaming responses
They measure the same thing in different units
explanation: Attention runs across the whole prompt at once; generation is sequential. Lesson 9.3 builds latency budgets from both.

stem: What does prompt caching (Lesson 5.5) reuse under the hood?
options: The keys and values computed for an unchanged prompt prefix — the KV cache
The previous answer
The tokeniser's merge table
The embedding of the user's name
explanation: If the prefix has not changed, its attention keys/values need not be recomputed. This is why only stable prefixes are cacheable.

stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes the two places knowledge can be?
options: Public vs private training data
Parametric (in the weights, fixed at training) vs in-context (in the prompt, supplied by you)
Short-term vs long-term memory inside the model
Cached vs uncached
explanation: RAG moves facts into the prompt; fine-tuning tries to add to the weights; prompting arranges the prompt so attention finds it.

options: Self-attention followed by a feed-forward layer, stacked many times
A tokeniser followed by a database lookup
A recurrent loop over characters
An embedding table and nothing else
explanation: Attention mixes information across tokens; the feed-forward layer transforms each token on its own and holds most stored knowledge.

stem: Your assistant 'forgets' instructions given ten turns ago. Which fix is most consistent with this lesson?
options: Pin the instructions in the system prompt or a facts block that is re-sent every turn
Ask the model to try harder to remember
Increase temperature so it explores earlier turns
Switch to a model with a larger vocabulary
explanation: Only what is in the current prompt is reachable. Instructions that must persist must be re-sent, ideally at the start (Lesson 2.5).
